newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to lift overseas stock futures ban in April.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to lift overseas stock futures ban in April.

text.p: Taiwan said on Wednesday it would lift a ban on local trading of offshore Taiwan stock-index futures in April, laying itself bare to overseas competition for months before its own planned exchange can open.
Finance Minister Paul Chiu, ending a day of uncertainty over when or even if Taiwan would legalise access to the offshore contracts, said the liberalisation had been approved.
"The Taiwan Stock Exchange will launch stock warrants in April before the offshore stock-index futures are approved, but both will be approved in April," Chiu told reporters.
Chiu had created the uncertainty earlier in the day when he gave what some lawmakers called a non-committal expression of support for lifting the ban.

Under the liberalisation, Taiwan futures houses for the first time will be able to trade futures linked to Taiwan stock market performance offered by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and Singapore International Monetary Exchange.

The CME and SIMEX launched the contracts on January 9 over the objections of Taiwan market regulators, who had pleaded in vain for them to wait until Taipei could open its own futures market and launch its own stock index contracts.

Under a Futures Trading Law enacted by parliament on Tuesday after years of bickering and delays, the exchange can open no sooner than October -- giving the SIMEX and CME at least a five-month window of opportunity to attract Taiwanese customers.
Singapore traders and analysts said the SIMEX likely would benefit most from Taiwan's liberalisation. Officials of the CME, its main rival, were not available for immediate comment.
SIMEX Taiwan-contract volume would "at least double," said Perry Gilbert, vice president of Refco (Singapore) Pte Ltd.
"Taiwanese retail punters who control 95 percent of the volume will clearly go to SIMEX," said Richard Fan, associate director of equity derivatives at W.I. Carr in Hong Kong.
Taiwan futures traders said the SIMEX appeared to have taken an early lead in terms of market, but that the CME could muscle back in with aggressive marketing once the ban is lifted.

Taiwan's futures exchange will offer the only futures linked directly to the Taiwan Stock Exchange's proprietary TAIEX index -- something local futures dealers say will give its contracts a big competitive edge over the offshore rivals.
The CME futures are based on Dow Jones & Co's Taiwan Index while the SIMEX uses Morgan Stanley's Taiwan Index Both claim to correlate highly to the TAIEX.

Taiwan's watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission has said its main concern in considering the liberalisation was whether the offshore contracts are traded at volumes large enough to ensure healthy market liquidity.
Commission officials said trading volume at both exchanges had been found to be acceptable, but declined to say what the benchmark level was.
"The liquidity of both the Singapore and Chicago Taiwan stock-index futures is fine," one commission official said.

Local futures houses are allowed to sell a range of overseas futures contracts, but Taiwan has balked at allowing trading of the SIMEX and CME contracts -- to date the only futures linked directly to Taiwan's own financial performance.

Many local investors are believed to be skirting the ban by placing orders through offshore brokers, a practice that has compounded pressure on Taiwan to launch its own futures or at least to allow access to the offshore Taiwan index contracts.
